title: Vandalism
summary: Vandalism and desecration have damaged sacred, burial, historical, and archaeological places, making preservation and careful stewardship necessary.
content:
Introduction

Vandalism, looting, careless collecting, and public curiosity have damaged sacred places, burial grounds, archaeological sites, and historic landscapes across Long Island. These harms are not only damage to objects or soil. They can disturb ancestors, erase evidence, violate community responsibilities, and make already vulnerable places more exposed.

Public education should protect sensitive places from digging, collecting, or trespass. Locations on the map are intentionally broad when needed, especially for burial places, ceremonial landscapes, private property, and archaeological sites.

Preservation depends on respect: do not dig, collect, remove, share sensitive directions, or disturb possible cultural material. When something is encountered, the responsible action is to leave it in place and contact the appropriate tribal, local, or state preservation authority.

Learning Questions

  • Why can public curiosity become harmful at burial or archaeological places?
  • What is the difference between learning from a site and disturbing it?
  • How can museums, towns, schools, and visitors support protection instead of extraction?
